 Plus: Northwood's Space Force milestone | Tuesday, November 24, 2026 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 View in browser 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 PRESENTED BY NORTHROP GRUMMAN 
 
 
   
 
 
 Axios Future of Defense 
 
 
 
 
 By Colin Demarest · Nov 24, 2026 
 
 
 G'morning! Thanks, again, to everyone who tuned in for the FoD Summit.

 And, ICYMI: We're doubling down on Huntsville , including a multiday Axios House event in the spring. Stay tuned for more details . 🤝 Situational awareness: U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting visited Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara in Kyiv. They discussed building Ukrainian drones in Britain, and the needed infrastructure.

 Farm to table: Boeing's "gasp"-worthy designs, Dutch F-35s in Finland and Thanksgiving grocery lists.

 Today's newsletter is 1,585 words, a 6-minute read. 

 
 
   
 
   
 
 
 1 big thing: "Talk about boats" 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 A GARC drone boat, moored at the Aevex Maritime Systems facility. Photo: Colin Demarest/Axios

 
 
 
   
 
 BALTIMORE — Fifteen minutes southeast of Camden Yards, between heavy industrial tracts and sprawling parking lots plastered with warning signs, sit rows and rows of shiny silver drone boats.

 Here, Aevex Maritime Systems is building and arming futuristic vessels capable of carrying everything from laser dazzlers to radars, from Joint Air-to-Ground Missiles to thousands of gallons of diesel fuel. "I'm a shipbuilder kind of guy," Todd Greene, vice president of maritime engineering, told reporters as he weaved between containers, trailers and trucks. "I can talk about boats all day." Why it matters: Militaries around the world are betting their futures on uncrewed vessels, citing Ukraine's success in using them to fend off Russia's far larger war machine.

 The U.S. in particular has talked about a hybrid fleet, or robotic-and-autonomous systems (RAS), for years. Aevex Maritime Systems is one of many players contributing to that vision — and competing for its precious dollars. Driving the news: A small group of journalists last week visited the company's production facilities and dock and went onto the Patapsco River, north of the wrecked Francis Scott Key Bridge, to watch some boats maneuver.

 A GARC catches air on the Patapsco River near Point Breeze. Photo: Colin Demarest/Axios Zoom in: On water and land, riding the waves or shielded by welding screens, were vessels in various stages of construction, upgrading and storage. They included:

 Global Autonomous Reconnaissance Craft (GARC), 15 feet, 8 inches: Used by the Navy and part of Operation Epic Fury in Iran. Chaser, 16 feet, 3 inches: In service with the Coast Guard and recently tested in San Diego. Comet, 43 feet: Perhaps the most menacing-looking, displayed at a Maryland defense conference with Sierra Nevada's BRAWLR air-defense weaponry aboard . NightTrain, 85 feet: A low-profile vessel that can ferry ISO containers and is sought by what Greene described as a "sustainment side" military logistics customer. Seabased Petroleum Distribution System, 200 feet: A concealable, offshore gas station backed this year by a $256 million contract. What they're saying: "There are, at this site, 60 different programs that are executing right now," Tim O'Connor, vice president of maritime growth, told reporters.

 "Unmanned surface vessels are probably the largest revenue generator for us right now, but I don't necessarily have to plan for that in the future," he said. "I need to be more broad than looking at just Navy and PAE RAS as a customer," he continued. "NightTrain is a bet toward the future. Comet is a bet toward the future." Headed southeast. Photo: Colin Demarest/Axios State of play: Aevex's acquisition of BlackSea Technologies gave rise to Maritime Systems. The deal, initially valued at up to $650 million, closed in early September.

 Follow the money: Aevex's stock ( AVEX ) tumbled a little more than a month later, after Bloomberg reported the Navy had no plans for additional GARC orders and that the boats were "troubled."

 The company quickly disputed "recent reports" in its own statement , and said an existing contract had been modified multiple times, increasing the total value to $350 million and extending the timeline. "We're operating them all over the world," O'Connor said, "and payloads are still going." What we're watching: Two straits — Hormuz and Taiwan — where drone boats are expected to make all the difference.

 More from Axios: 

 The Navy's chaotic aircraft carrier news cycle 

 Introducing Trump's puzzling nuclear-armed battleship 

 Drone boat rescues U.S. helicopter crew shot down by Iran 

 
 
   
 
   
 
 
 2. Scoop: Northwood milestone 
 
 By Thomas Novelly 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Northwood Space Portal units in California were used for a September test. Photo: Courtesy of Northwood Space

 
 
 
   
 
 Northwood Space quickly connected its antennas with a satellite in deep orbit during a Space Force test, a key milestone first shared with Axios.

 Why it matters: The U.S. military wants rapidly deployable, survivable and reliable ground stations for future conflicts.

 In September, as part of a Space Force prototype contract, Northwood's Portal ground antennas connected multiple times and exchanged data simultaneously with a U.S. government satellite in geosynchronous orbit, or GEO. Satellites in GEO move in tandem with the Earth's rotation, providing wider coverage for military operations. After the successful Space Force test, the Torrance, California-based firm's Portal antenna is now eligible for the Space Force to move it from prototype into production. What she's saying: "GEO satellites carry some of the most critical government and commercial missions, and they're some of the hardest links to close," Bridgit Mendler, Northwood's CEO, said in a statement.

 Read the full story . 

 
 
   
 
   
 
 
 3. Summit catch-up 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Great minds. Screenshot: Axios/via YouTube 

 
 
 
   
 
 More than a dozen interviews. Plenty of builders. A few financiers. Two lawmakers. And one jet-powered drone .

 The third annual Future of Defense Summit is a wrap. The big picture: Here are some moments you may have missed Nov. 19 :

 😮 Boeing defense boss Steve Parker anticipates people will "gasp" when the company's sixth-generation Air Force F-47 and Navy F/A-XX are publicly revealed.

 "We're very confident in the technology we've brought to bear on both proposals," he said. "We wouldn't have bid both if we didn't believe we could execute both." 💤 Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) said the White House has been silent about the holdup of a $14 billion weapons package lawmakers approved months ago for Taiwan.

 "We need to investigate and bring people in and make it transparent as to what has actually taken place over the last two years," he said. "Once the 120th Congress takes place, we're going to do a lot of traveling." 🧊 Davie Defense chief executive Philip Burns-O'Brien said the five icebreakers his company is building for the U.S. Coast Guard are on schedule, with the first ship to be constructed in 26 months.

 "We're confident that we can deliver, because we've got the experience," he said. "We're doing things differently than we traditionally do in the U.S." 🧨 Ross Fubini, managing partner at XYZ Venture Capital, said he still regrets not investing in Castelion, the hypersonic missile startup making Blackbeard.

 "We were talking to them ... and then we just whiffed it," he said. 👏 Twenty CEO Joe Lin said the Trump administration "deserves a ton of credit" for "how much more publicly" it's talked "about the need for offensive cyber."

 "That need has always been there," he said, but there's been "a self-imposed constraint on our willingness to admit we have this requirement, and the fact that we do it." 🗺️ Miles Arnone, the co-founder of Re:Build, said he would urge President Trump not to use tariffs as a "cudgel against our allies. Let's be consistent."

 "No one's going to invest behind a highly volatile tariff — or any regulatory regime," he said. "I would ask for stability, if that's possible." Go deeper: Defense-tech diversifies as "voracious" investors pour in 

 
 
   
 
   
A MESSAGE FROM NORTHROP GRUMMAN

 
 Sentinel is standing tall — and getting close to flight testing 
   
 
 
 
   
 
 As Sentinel moves from development toward deployment, the stakes are clear: a modern nuclear deterrent is essential to keeping the U.S. and its allies safe. Northrop Grumman is driving rapid progress to deliver a system built for decades of deterring evolving threats.


 Read more on our progress. 


 
   
 
   
 
 
 4. Quick hits 
 
 By Colin Demarest and Thomas Novelly 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Touching down on a Finnish highway. Photo: Courtesy of the Dutch defense ministry

 
 
 
   
 
 🛣️ Several Dutch F-35s landed on a major highway in Finland during the Protective Fence exercise this month. The defense ministry said in a translated statement it shows how the Royal Netherlands Air and Space Force "is less dependent on fixed bases."

 Why it matters: Wars in Eastern Europe and the Middle East have reinforced just how quickly military infrastructure gets cratered. 💭 My thought bubble: This also looks mega cool . 🚀 Back-to-back SpaceX Falcon 9 launches for the U.S. National Reconnaissance Office and Space Force made history Sunday.

 Why it matters: Both missions were from the same launchpad at California's Vandenberg Space Force Base within 32 hours of each other, marking the company's fastest turnaround ever. 💭 My thought bubble: It's a milestone to celebrate — but also shows how reliant the military is on a reusable rocket that may be retired. 🐬 Odin Dynamics emerged from stealth with $17 million, including an almost $14 million seed. Backers include Freestyle VC, BlueYard Capital and Sierra Ventures. The startup makes "robotic underwater vehicles."

 Why it matters: "When I was on active duty, drones saved my life in Iraq, at least twice," COO Jon Haase told me. "As a founder, all I care about is winning, and winning means America wins and Americans make it home." 💭 My thought bubble: Tectonic broke the news, here . 🇫🇷 French launch provider Arianespace announced it experienced a technical problem on Monday that pushed back a mission to place Amazon Leo satellites in orbit. 

 Why it matters: Arianespace is another one of the launch providers for Amazon's emerging satellite internet service, a SpaceX Starlink competitor. 💭 My thought bubble: After ULA's mishap earlier this month , this marks another tough situation for Amazon and further illustrates launch woes for the commercial space industry. 
 
   
 
   
 
 
 5. Check this out 
 
 By Colin Demarest and Thomas Novelly 
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Thanksgiving lunch for U.S. soldiers at Caserma Ederle, Italy. Photo: Brian Andries/DVIDS

 
 
 
   
 
 You think you bought a lot of groceries for Thanksgiving ? Consider this.

 The U.S. Defense Logistics Agency told us it has procured for the upcoming holiday:

 🦃 193,459 pounds of turkey (includes whole and roasted)

 🥩 162,079 pounds of beef

 🦀 128,488 pounds of crab, lobster and shrimp

 🍖 86,938 pounds of ham (includes bone-in, pork loin and hock)

 🐷 14,896 pounds of whole pig

 🥧 8,018 cases of pies and cakes

 🥫 7,158 cans of sweet potatoes

 🥛 1,321 cases of eggnog

 Our thought bubble: This feels like the "55 burgers, 55 fries, 55 tacos" bit .

 The bottom line: Ham is better than turkey, and mac and cheese is the superior side, says Colin. Turkey is the top-tier protein, and sweet potato pie is better than pumpkin , according to Tom.

 
 
   
 
   
A MESSAGE FROM NORTHROP GRUMMAN

 
 America is inventing what's next — and building it at scale 
   
 
 
 
   
 
 The technologies shaping the future fight must move quickly from bold ideas to production at scale. Northrop Grumman combines unmatched depth of innovation with 30 million square feet of U.S. manufacturing capacity to build what’s next, faster.


 See what's behind our performance. 


 
   
 
 Shoutout to Mike Zapler for editing and Matt Piper for copy editing. 

 Don't forget: No Thursday edition this week! 

 👋🏼 Thanks, as always, for reading and sharing. Tell your friends to subscribe here .
